label: Anger
title: Bhagavad Gita on Anger: 7 Verses to Cool a Temper
description: Seven verses on anger: how it starts (2.62 and 2.63), how to ride out the surge (5.23) and how to speak after (17.15). Sanskrit, plain English and one thing to try.
h1: Bhagavad Gita on anger: 7 verses to cool a temper
subtitle: For when your temper gets there before you do. Read one a day, or all seven while you cool off.
keywords: how to control anger bhagavad gita
intro: In 2.62 and 2.63 the Gita traces anger step by step: dwelling on something becomes attachment, attachment becomes wanting, blocked wanting becomes anger, and anger takes judgement with it. These verses walk that chain slowly, then turn to the steady mind, riding out the surge (5.23) and speech that doesn't wound (17.15). The last is from the Ramayana, a sage who lost his temper, lost years of work, and began again. This plan is for the anger you want to stop acting on. If someone is harming you, you are right to name it.

days.heading: Where anger starts
days.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
days.forYou: Krishna starts earlier than the outburst. Dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ: when you keep dwelling on something, you get attached, attachment turns into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall turns into anger. By the time you snap, the fire has been building for a while.
days.today: After your next flash of irritation, trace it back one step: what were you dwelling on?

days.heading: What anger takes from you
days.line: Anger clouds judgement, clouded judgement loses memory, lost memory wrecks reason, and then you fall.
days.forYou: From anger comes confusion, then memory slips, then judgement goes, and then you fall. Krishna's word for that last step is praṇaśyati. You say the thing you can't take back, because the part of you that knew better has already left the room.
days.today: Recall one argument you regret. Find the moment judgement left. What came just before it?
days.note: Feeling anger is human. The warning is about anger that takes over your judgement.

days.heading: Know the real enemy
days.line: Desire, turning to anger when blocked and never satisfied, is the real enemy here.
days.forYou: Arjuna asks why we do wrong against our own will. Krishna names desire, which turns into anger when it's blocked and is never satisfied. When you're angry at someone, look for what you wanted from them.
days.today: When you're angry today, finish this sentence: what I wanted was…

days.heading: A steady mind still feels
days.line: Unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, free of clinging, fear and anger: that is a steady mind.
days.forYou: Krishna's portrait of the steady person: unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, free of clinging, fear and anger. This person still feels everything. The feelings just don't get to drive.
days.today: Picture the calmest person you know in your hardest situation. What would they do first?

days.heading: Ride out the surge
days.line: Whoever can ride out the surge of desire and anger, here and now, is steady and happy.
days.forYou: Krishna says whoever can withstand the surge (vega) of desire and anger, here in this life, is steady and happy. A surge rises and falls. Your only job is to wait until it passes before you act.
days.today: Next time the surge comes, let ten slow breaths pass before you speak or type.

days.heading: Then speak
days.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
days.forYou: Krishna calls it the discipline of speech: words that don't agitate, that are true, pleasant and helpful. Your anger often has a point. This verse shows how to make that point without cruelty, once the surge has passed.
days.today: Rewrite one message you sent in anger. Keep what's true. Drop what was meant to hurt.
days.note: Kind speech can still say hard things. It says them without cruelty.

days.heading: He lost his temper, and began again

story.title: Vishvamitra's vow
story.body: Vishvamitra had given up a kingdom to become a sage, and had already started his effort over more than once. Then, tested again, he lost his temper and cursed the apsara Rambha, and with that curse the power of his long austerity was spent. This time he made a vow: he would not give way to anger, or even speak. He kept a long silence. Obstacles came again and shook him, but anger couldn't get in. In the end he reached his goal, and Vasishtha, the rival he had once fought, embraced him as a friend.
story.lesson: Relapses happen. A clear vow and steady practice can loosen anger's grip.

days.forYou: If you've promised yourself before and blown it, you're in Vishvamitra's company. His story keeps going after the relapse.
days.today: Make one specific vow for this week, such as 'I won't send messages while angry', and tell one person.

verse.sanskrit: पूर्णे वर्षसहस्रे तु काष्ठभूतं महामुनिम् । विघ्नैर्बहुभिराधूतं क्रोधो नान्तरमाविशत् ॥
verse.line: Many things shook him. Anger could not get in.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about anger?
faq.a: In 2.62 and 2.63 Krishna traces anger from dwelling on something, to attachment, to desire, to anger, and from anger to confusion, lost memory, lost judgement and ruin. In 3.37 he names desire, which turns into anger, as the real enemy, and in 16.21 he calls lust, anger and greed the three gates to ruin.

faq.q: What is the meaning of krodhād bhavati sammohaḥ?
faq.a: It opens Bhagavad Gita 2.63: from anger comes delusion. The verse continues: from delusion, confusion of memory; from that, loss of judgement; and from loss of judgement, a person falls.

faq.q: How does the Gita say to control anger?
faq.a: By seeing it early (2.62), withstanding the surge before acting (5.23), and speaking only words that are true, kind and helpful (17.15). Krishna's steady person still feels anger and stays in charge of it (2.56).
